items.prompt: Which of these is an idle resource?
choices: A production database answering customer requests all day
A test database nobody has used since its project ended
A web server that handles the checkout page's traffic
A cache that makes the product pages load faster
items.explanation: An idle resource is still running and billing after its purpose has ended. The other three are all doing work.

items.prompt: Why do idle resources survive for so long?
choices: They are impossible to switch off once created
Nothing breaks when they keep running
They cost nothing until someone starts using them
The provider refuses to delete them for free
items.explanation: They never fail or slow anything down, so no alarm ever points at them.

items.prompt: When does the cloud charge for a resource?
choices: Only for hours when someone logs in to it
Only while it serves customer traffic
For every hour it exists, used or not
Once a month, for the busiest day only
items.explanation: Billing follows existence. That is why a forgotten resource keeps costing money.

items.prompt: Five test databases cost an assumed $400 each per month. What is the total?
choices: $1,600 a month
$2,400 a month
$4,000 a month
$2,000 a month
items.explanation: 5 x 400 = 2,000. This matches the forgotten-database line in the unit's bill.

items.prompt: Which habit most directly stops forgotten resources piling up?
choices: Tag every resource with an owner and an expiry date
Buy larger servers so none ever run out of space
Review the bill only once the quarter has ended
Give every team its own separate cloud account
items.explanation: An owner says who to ask, and an expiry says when to ask. Together they make forgetting visible.

items.prompt: A disk volume survives after its server is deleted. What is it now?
choices: Free, because nothing is attached to it any more
Deleted automatically within one billing hour
Likely idle, still billing, and easy to forget
Counted as part of the deleted server's cost
items.explanation: Volumes often outlive their servers and keep billing until someone deletes them.

items.prompt: In the tap story, what is the cloud equivalent of the dripping tap?
choices: A server restarting every night on a timer
A dashboard that loads slowly in the morning
A resource left running that nobody uses
A bill that arrives with a different logo
items.explanation: A drip makes no noise and the cost only shows later. An unused running resource behaves the same way.

items.prompt: What should the tag on a test database name?
choices: The vendor who invoices the account each month
The newest hire, so they learn the system
The server where the database is hosted
The person or team to ask before deleting it
items.explanation: The point of an owner tag is to know who can say whether something is still needed.

items.prompt: A team runs a one-off script that deletes every currently idle test database. Six months later a new pile has appeared. What did the script miss?
choices: It should have deleted the production databases as well
Nothing sets an owner or expiry at creation time
Test databases cannot safely be removed by any script
The provider recreates deleted resources every month
items.explanation: The script treated the symptom. As long as resources are created without an owner or expiry, forgotten ones keep accumulating.
items.reference:
An idle resource
🚰 still running, still billing
🎯 the purpose that justified it has ended
🔇 nothing breaks, so nobody looks
🏷️ fix: an owner and an expiry date
Why: billing follows existence, not use, so forgotten things keep costing.
items.learnMore:
Billing follows existence, not use

A cloud resource charges for every hour it exists. A test database, an old staging stack or an unattached disk keeps billing after its purpose ends, and because it never fails, nothing draws attention to it. The durable fix is a process: an owner and an expiry set at creation.

Common mistake

Treating cleanup as a one-time event. A single sweep fixes today's pile and leaves the cause untouched.
items.reflection: Think of something in your home that keeps costing money while unused (a subscription, a spare storage unit). What would be your equivalent of an owner and an expiry date for it?

items.prompt: A volume shows no reads for 90 days, but an audit job reads it once a quarter. What is the right move?
choices: Ask the owner first: quiet is not the same as finished
Delete it: a month without reads proves it is finished
Delete it: a quarterly job should not depend on it
Keep it forever: volumes can never be deleted once made
items.explanation: Low recent use is a hint, not proof. The owner tag exists so the person who knows the purpose makes the call.

items.prompt: What does right-sizing mean?
choices: Buying capacity to match measured peak usage plus a margin
Buying the smallest possible server for every job
Buying whatever size the vendor recommends
Buying the largest server to avoid any slowdown
items.explanation: Right-sizing starts from measurement and keeps a deliberate margin. It is neither the smallest nor the largest option.

items.prompt: Staging had 16 vCPU and needed 4 vCPU at its busiest. How many times too big was it?
choices: 2 times
4 times
8 times
16 times
items.explanation: 16 divided by 4 is 4.

items.prompt: Why was staging oversized?
choices: A teammate wanted to waste money on purpose
Cloud servers only come in the largest size
Smaller servers are not allowed for staging
The size was guessed before any usage data existed
items.explanation: Nobody was reckless. The guess was made early and never revisited.

items.prompt: At an assumed $225 per vCPU-month, what do 4 vCPU cost per month?
At an assumed $225 per vCPU-month, what do 16 vCPU cost per month?
What should a right-sized number be based on?
choices: What sounds safe on the day of purchase
What was measured, with a deliberate margin
What a large competitor is believed to use
What the previous team happened to buy
items.explanation: Measurement replaces guessing. The margin is then a decision, not an accident.

items.prompt: Which of these is a measurement and not a guess?
choices: A feeling that the app might get popular
The size of the server in the old plan
Peak CPU use over the last four weeks
A teammate's memory of one past outage
items.explanation: Only the first is observed data about how the resource is actually used.

items.prompt: Was the person who sized staging careless?
choices: No: the guess came before any data and was never revisited
Yes: sizing without data is always careless
No: servers cannot be resized after purchase
Yes: staging should always match production exactly
items.explanation: The failure was the missing revisit, which is why right-sizing is described as a loop later on.

items.prompt: Staging's busiest moment used 25 percent of its 16 vCPU. A teammate proposes exactly 4 vCPU to save the most. What is missing?
choices: A second staging environment to share the load evenly
A margin for a spike above anything measured so far
A larger server so that utilization looks higher
Approval from the vendor before reducing capacity
items.explanation: The measured peak is only the biggest spike seen so far. A margin is the decision about how much more to allow.
items.reference:
Right-sizing, in numbers
📦 bought: 16 vCPU = $3,600 a month (assumed)
📏 measured peak need: 4 vCPU = $900
🧮 gap: 4 times what the work required
➕ then add a deliberate margin
Why: capacity should follow measurement, not a number that merely sounded safe.
items.learnMore:
Measure first, then add a margin on purpose

Right-sizing buys capacity to match measured peak usage plus a chosen safety margin. The original guess is not a moral failing, it was made before data existed. The failure is never going back once data did exist.

Common mistake

Sizing to the average. The average hides the one busy hour the resource must survive.
items.reflection: Pick something you bought 'just in case' (a larger phone plan, a bigger suitcase). What would you need to measure to know whether the guess was right?

items.prompt: Two teams each pay for 16 vCPU. Team A measured a 4 vCPU peak, Team B a 15 vCPU peak. Which statement is right?
choices: Team A is over-provisioned; Team B is near its need
Both are over-provisioned, since 16 is always too many
Team B is over-provisioned because it uses more CPU
Both are right-sized because they pay the same price
items.explanation: Right-sizing compares capacity with measured need. The same price for different need means very different efficiency.

The minimum, since it shows the least it can need
The median, since it ignores unusual hours entirely
The peak, since the average hides the busy hour
items.explanation: The resource must survive its busiest hour. The average smooths that hour away.

items.prompt: Memory peaks at 60 percent of a server and CPU at 20 percent. What does shrinking by CPU alone risk?
choices: Freeing memory as well, since the two always move together
Raising CPU use to 100 percent, which is the real goal
Running out of memory, the dimension closest to its limit
Nothing at all, since memory is never a sizing factor
items.explanation: A resource is limited by whichever dimension is closest to saturation, so sizing must look at every dimension.

items.prompt: Why does a crashed service get noticed faster than a rising bill?
choices: A crash pages someone, while a bill pages nobody by default
A crash is always far larger than any bill
Bills can only be seen by the cloud vendor
Engineers are unable to observe anything but crashes
items.explanation: Alerts exist for failures. Spend has no alert unless someone builds one.

items.prompt: What is a budget?
choices: A forecast of next year's revenue
A committed spending ceiling for a period
A list of every server in the account
A discount negotiated with the vendor
items.explanation: A budget is the cost twin of a reliability target: a ceiling to check against.

items.prompt: What does a budget alert do?
choices: Pays the invoice automatically each month
Deletes resources once the budget is gone
Warns while there is still time to act
Raises the budget whenever spending grows
items.explanation: Its job is early warning, so a person can decide before the ceiling is hit.

items.prompt: In the tap story, when does the first signal arrive?
choices: Day 2, with a sound
Day 1, from the tap itself
Never, because the tap stops
Day 30, with the bill
items.explanation: The drip is silent. Only the bill, after the month, tells the story.

items.prompt: Which tool shows where the money goes?
choices: A chart of response times by page
A dashboard of spend by resource
A list of open pull requests
A graph of errors by status code
items.explanation: Spend by resource answers 'what is costing us' the way an error graph answers 'what is failing'.

items.prompt: What makes cost visibility different from CPU monitoring by default?
choices: It is impossible to build for cloud accounts
Someone must decide to build it, as it is not automatic
It only works after the invoice has arrived
It is built into every server automatically
items.explanation: CPU graphs come with most platforms. Spend signals usually need to be set up deliberately.

items.prompt: An alert fires on day 2 instead of an invoice on day 30. How many days earlier is that?
choices: 26 days
30 days
28 days
32 days
items.explanation: 30 minus 2 is 28.

items.prompt: A spend dashboard opened once a month is best described as...
choices: An early warning of next week's bill
A guard that stops spending at a limit
A forecast of next quarter's usage
A look back at money already spent
items.explanation: Looking monthly only shows the past. Early warning needs an alert during the month.

items.prompt: A team has a spend dashboard and a monthly budget, but nothing fires during the month. What is still missing?
choices: A larger budget, so that the ceiling is never reached at all
A forecast alert that warns before the ceiling is reached
A second dashboard that shows the very same totals
A rule that bans anyone creating any new resource
items.explanation: A dashboard and a budget describe the situation. Only an alert interrupts someone while action is still possible.
items.reference:
Cost visibility, the missing signal
📉 crash: pages someone within minutes
🧾 bill: pages nobody until the invoice
📊 dashboard: where the money goes
🔔 budget alert: warns while there is time
Why: a signal that arrives after the money is spent cannot prevent anything.
items.learnMore:
Nobody pages you about money

Reliability signals get built because an outage hurts at once. Spend signals are optional until a bill hurts. Cost visibility means building them on purpose: a dashboard by resource, a budget as a ceiling, and an alert that fires during the month.

Common mistake

Assuming that checking the invoice counts as monitoring. It is a report on spending that already happened.
items.reflection: Where in your own life do you only learn the total after it is too late to change it (a card statement, a data plan)? What early signal would help?

items.prompt: Which signal shows a cost problem soonest?
choices: A forecast of month-end spend passing the budget
Total spend so far having reached the full budget
The invoice arriving on the first of the month
A teammate mentioning that the bill felt high
items.explanation: The forecast looks ahead using the pace. The other signals only appear once money is already spent.

items.prompt: What are the four steps of the right-sizing loop?
choices: Measure, size, set budget and alert, re-audit
Guess, buy, deploy, wait for the next invoice
Size, measure, delete, rebuild from scratch
Budget, buy, scale up, scale up again
items.explanation: The loop is measure, size, protect with a budget and alert, then re-audit.

items.prompt: Which step makes it a loop and not a one-time exercise?
choices: Measure once on day one
Buy the biggest size once
Re-audit on a schedule
Delete the old servers once
items.explanation: Without the re-audit, the process ends after one pass and goes stale.

items.prompt: Why does usage need re-auditing?
choices: Servers shrink by themselves each month
Vendors change their prices every single week
Traffic, team and product change over time
Old measurements expire after exactly 24 hours
items.explanation: Usage drifts, so yesterday's measurement stops describing today.

items.prompt: A quarterly load test needs 12 vCPU for 2 days; normal use is 4 vCPU. What is the sensible plan?
choices: Run 12 vCPU all quarter to be safe
Run 4 vCPU and cancel the load test
Run 2 vCPU and hope the test still finishes
Run 4 vCPU and add capacity for the two test days
items.explanation: A two-day need is a reason to scale up for two days, not to pay for the peak all quarter.

items.prompt: Permanent peak sizing for a two-day need is...
choices: Over-provisioning with a respectable-looking number
The cheapest option in every case
Required by the cloud provider
A way to avoid measuring usage
items.explanation: It is the same 'just in case' mistake, only with a measured peak attached.

items.prompt: What does 12 vCPU cost for 3 months at an assumed $225 per vCPU-month?
What comes right after right-sizing in the loop?
choices: Measure usage for the very first time
Delete last month's budget entirely
Raise the ceiling on auto-scaling
Set a budget and alert on the new size
items.explanation: The alert watches the new baseline, so it follows the resize.

items.prompt: Which of these is measured at the start of the loop?
choices: The price on the vendor's home page
The number of engineers on the team
The age of the company's cloud account
CPU, memory and storage use over weeks
items.explanation: The loop starts from how the resource is really used.

items.prompt: Staging needs 4 vCPU normally and 12 vCPU for 2 days a quarter, at an assumed $225 per vCPU-month. What does the scale-up plan cost per quarter?
items.explanation: 4 x 225 x 3 = 2,700, plus 8 extra vCPU for 2 of 30 days: 8 x 225 x 2/30 = 120. Total 2,820.
items.reference:
The right-sizing loop
📐 1. measure usage over weeks
📏 2. size to peak plus margin
🔔 3. budget and alert on the new size
🔁 4. re-audit on a schedule, back to 1
Why: usage drifts, so a size chosen once goes stale like the first guess.
items.learnMore:
A loop, not a snapshot

Measure, size, set the budget and alert, and re-audit. The re-audit is what turns the steps into a loop. A rare peak, such as a two-day load test, is handled by scaling up for those days rather than paying for the peak all quarter.

Common mistake

Sizing permanently to the rarest peak. It feels safe and quietly costs several times more.
items.reflection: Think of a habit you set up once and never reviewed (a thermostat schedule, a phone plan). What would a sensible 're-audit' date look like?

items.prompt: A re-audit finds usage doubled since the last quarter. What does the loop say to do?
choices: Resize to the new peak plus margin and update the alert
Keep the old size and raise the alert threshold to match
Delete the audit because the result is inconvenient
Double the size permanently and stop measuring
items.explanation: The loop responds to new data by sizing again and moving the alert with it.

items.prompt: What makes unbounded auto-scaling a cost risk?
choices: Nothing stops it adding servers as demand or a bug grows
It always adds fewer servers than needed
It removes servers during the busiest periods
It sends the bill to the wrong account
items.explanation: Without a limit, the bill follows the load wherever it goes, including load caused by a bug.

items.prompt: What is a ceiling on an auto-scaling group?
choices: A minimum number of servers it must run
A maximum number of servers it may run
The price of a single server per hour
The time of day scaling is allowed
items.explanation: The ceiling is the upper limit on the group's size.

items.prompt: A group runs 4 servers normally and 18 during a storm. At an assumed $200 per server-month, what is the extra cost per month?
A ceiling of 8 servers at an assumed $200 each. What is the worst-case monthly cost?
items.explanation: 8 x 200 = 1,600 if the group sat at the ceiling all month.

items.prompt: What should accompany a ceiling?
choices: An alert when the group reaches it
A second ceiling set much higher
A rule hiding the group's metrics
A script that deletes the group monthly
items.explanation: The alert tells a person the group has hit its limit, so they can decide what to do.

items.prompt: Which event can push a group to many servers without anyone intending it?
choices: A teammate renaming a server
A retry bug that multiplies requests
A new color theme on the dashboard
A new logo on the home page
items.explanation: Retries multiply real load, so the group scales to meet it.

items.prompt: Why does a group sitting silently at its ceiling matter?

It lowers the bill to zero
Nobody learns that demand has outgrown it
It means the ceiling is set too high

items.prompt: Which of these is a known worst case?
choices: A bill with no ceiling during a retry storm
A bill measured only after the month ends
A bill that depends on the account's limits
A bill capped by a ceiling of 12 servers
items.explanation: A ceiling converts 'unknown' into a figure you can compute.

items.prompt: Why is a ceiling alone not enough?
choices: Ceilings stop a group from ever scaling down again
Silent saturation hides that demand outgrew it
Ceilings raise the price of each individual server
Ceilings only work for databases and not for servers
items.explanation: A group that quietly pins at its maximum looks calm while users may suffer. The alert is what exposes it.
items.reference:
Ceiling plus alert
⚙️ group: 4 servers normally, $200 each (assumed)
🌩️ retry storm pushes it to 18
➕ extra: (18 - 4) x 200 = $2,800 a month
🛑 ceiling caps it, an alert tells a person
Why: a ceiling turns an open-ended bill into a known worst case.
items.learnMore:
Auto-scaling needs a ceiling and an alert

Auto-scaling is useful because it adds capacity on demand. Without a ceiling it will also add capacity for a bug. A ceiling gives a worst-case bill, and an alert makes sure someone learns the group has reached it.

Common mistake

Setting the ceiling as low as possible. Real demand above it is then refused, which is a reliability failure.

items.prompt: Spend so far is 8,000 on day 10 of 30. What is the daily pace?
items.explanation: 8,000 divided by 10 is 800.

items.prompt: A pace of 800 a day over a 30-day month gives a forecast of...
Which number should be compared with the budget?
choices: The spend so far today
Last month's invoice total
The forecast for the end of the period
The number of days left
items.explanation: The forecast shows where the month is heading, with time still left to react.

items.prompt: Phone data: 8 GB used by day 10 of a 30-day month. What is the pace?
choices: 0.3 GB a day
1.0 GB a day
8 GB a day
0.8 GB a day
items.explanation: 8 divided by 10 is 0.8.

items.prompt: Why can a forecast warn earlier than the spend so far?
choices: It uses the pace, so it turns red with days left to act
It waits until the money is already gone
It counts only the weekends of the month
It ignores the budget completely
items.explanation: The total only crosses the budget at the end. The pace shows the problem on day 10.

items.prompt: A healthy month spent 3,000 by day 10 of 30. What is the forecast?
items.explanation: 3,000 divided by 10 is 300 a day, times 30 is 9,000.

items.prompt: What does an escalate verdict at 110 percent mean?
choices: Spend so far is at least 110 percent of budget
The budget will be raised by 110 percent
The forecast is at least 110 percent of the budget
The pace is 110 dollars a day
items.explanation: The threshold applies to the forecast as a share of budget.

items.prompt: About what daily pace uses a 10,000 budget exactly over 30 days?
items.explanation: 10,000 divided by 30 is about 333.

items.prompt: Days 1 to 7 cost 200 a day and days 8 to 10 cost 600 a day. For a 10,000 budget over 30 days, what is the forecast at the trailing 3-day pace?
items.explanation: Spent so far is 1,400 + 1,800 = 3,200. Add 20 days at 600 = 12,000, giving 15,200.
items.reference:
Pace, then forecast
📅 10,000 budget, 30 days, 8,000 spent on day 10
➗ pace = 8,000 / 10 = 800 a day
✖️ forecast = 800 x 30 = 24,000
⚖️ compare the forecast, not the total so far
Why: how much is used cannot answer whether it will run out; only the pace can.
items.learnMore:
Compare the pace, not the total

Spend so far is a past fact. The forecast projects the pace to the end of the period. A whole-period average is stable but slow to notice a recent jump, so a short trailing window is a useful second view.

Common mistake

Waiting for spend so far to reach the budget. By then the month is nearly gone.
items.reflection: Choose a limit in your life that resets (monthly data, a weekly food budget). On day 10 of 30, what pace tells you whether you will stay under it?

items.prompt: Why can a whole-period average understate a recent change in spend?

It counts each day twice, which lowers the daily total
It ignores the most recent three days of spend entirely
It converts dollars into a lower-value currency first
items.explanation: Averaging weights old and new days equally, so a fresh jump moves the average only slowly.

items.prompt: Staging needs 4 vCPU at peak. With a 2.0x margin, how many vCPU are needed?
Servers come in whole units. A need of 5.2 vCPU means you buy...
items.explanation: You cannot buy a fraction, and rounding down would cut the margin.

items.prompt: At an assumed $225 per vCPU-month, what do 6 vCPU cost?
What can go wrong if you size to exactly the measured peak?
choices: The bill rises above the original guess
The resource turns itself off every night
Measurements stop being collected
A new higher spike saturates the resource
items.explanation: The measured peak is only the biggest spike seen so far.

items.prompt: What can go wrong with an auto-scaling ceiling set too low?
choices: Real demand is capped and users see slowness
The bill grows without any upper limit
Idle resources are no longer found
Budget alerts stop working
items.explanation: A ceiling below real demand turns a cost guardrail into a slowdown.

items.prompt: Why do cost and reliability pull in opposite directions?
choices: Cheaper servers are always more reliable
More spare capacity costs more but protects users
Reliability work never costs any money
Budgets only apply to unreliable systems
items.explanation: Spare capacity is the shared object: it costs money and protects users.

items.prompt: Alerts that fire on every small bump lead to...
choices: Faster fixes, since people react to each
Lower bills, since people feel watched
Being ignored, so the real one is missed
No change, since alerts are decoration
items.explanation: Alert fatigue makes people tune out the one that matters.

items.prompt: In the margin table, what does the 4.0x row represent?
choices: The original guess, which saves nothing
The cheapest option available
A margin that is too small
The safest sensible option for any case
items.explanation: 4 x 4 = 16 vCPU at $3,600 is where staging started, so the saving is zero.

items.prompt: A need of 4 vCPU at peak with a 1.6x margin, at an assumed $225 per vCPU-month, buying whole vCPU. What is the monthly cost?
items.explanation: 4 x 1.6 = 6.4, rounded up to 7 vCPU. 7 x 225 = 1,575.
items.reference:
Margin table (4 vCPU measured, $225 each)
1.0x: 4 vCPU = $900, no cushion
1.3x: 5.2, buy 6 = $1,350
2.0x: 8 vCPU = $1,800
4.0x: 16 vCPU = $3,600, the original guess
Why: each guardrail, pushed too far, creates the failure it was meant to prevent.
items.learnMore:
Cost and reliability pull in opposite directions

A margin is a price paid for safety. Too little and a new spike saturates the resource. Too much and the saving disappears. The same holds for a ceiling that is too low and for an alert that fires on every bump.

Common mistake

Reading the lowest bill as the best outcome. It may simply be the one with the least safety.
items.reflection: In a system you know (a kitchen, a school bus fleet, a laptop battery), where is the spare capacity? What would 'trimmed too far' look like there?

items.prompt: Why does the sizing rule round up to whole vCPU?

Servers can only be bought in odd-numbered counts
Rounding has no effect on either capacity or cost
items.explanation: The margin is a floor. Rounding down quietly gives part of it away for a small, certain saving.
